<!-- Generated by website/sync-docs.py from docs/raid.md. Edit that file, not this one. -->

Corium can build software RAID arrays from the spare disks of a node. You
declare them in the same `corium:` block as all other configuration. To put the
root filesystem on RAID is a different problem with a different answer. This
page covers both.

---

## Two problems, not one

| | Spare disks | Root filesystem |
|---|---|---|
| Declared in `corium:` | yes, `raid[]` | no |
| When it happens | first boot | install time |
| Install paths | every one | ISO / bare metal only |
| Mechanism | `corium-agent` runs `mdadm` | Anaconda Kickstart |

This split is not a design preference. It is a consequence of the boot order.
When the node reads the `corium:` block, the root filesystem is already
deployed and mounted. The process that reads the block runs from it. At that
point, nothing can move the root filesystem onto an array. Only the tool that
first wrote the disk can make a redundant root, and that tool is the installer.

---

## Spare disks

```yaml
#cloud-config
corium:
  role: controller+worker
  raid:
    - name: data
      level: 1
      devices:
        - /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1
        - /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi2
      filesystem: ext4
      mountPoint: /var/lib/corium/data
```

At first boot, the node builds `/dev/md/data`, formats it, and mounts it. It
writes an `/etc/fstab` entry so that later boots also mount it. It records the
array in `/etc/mdadm.conf` so that the array reassembles.

The [configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration/#311-raid) lists every field.

### Use `/dev/disk/by-id`

The kernel gives names such as `/dev/sdb` and `/dev/sdc` in discovery order.
That order can change on the next boot. On a first boot, the order can also be
different from the order you expected when you wrote the configuration. To
build an array destroys the data on its disks, so the wrong disk name causes
serious loss.

A `/dev/disk/by-id/...` path names the hardware. Use it.

### It refuses to destroy data

The bootstrap stops if a device already holds a filesystem, a partition table,
or the metadata of another array:

```
device /dev/sdb already holds a filesystem or array member signature (TYPE=ext4);
refusing to overwrite it. Set wipe: true on this array to consent to erasing
these devices
```

`wipe: true` gives your consent. It is off by default because the two failures
do not cost the same. A node that does not finish its bootstrap costs you an
afternoon. A disk that Corium erased without a warning cannot be recovered,
however careful you are afterwards.

If you run the bootstrap again on a node where the array already exists, the
node adopts the array. It does not rebuild the array, and it does not reformat
a filesystem that is already on it.

### How this differs from `runcmd` + `mdadm`

cloud-init has no RAID support. Its `disk_setup` module makes partitions and
filesystems. For years, its documentation said that mdadm support is planned.
So the real alternative to this feature is a `runcmd` block that calls `mdadm`
by hand. That approach gets three things wrong.

**The array exists before k0s starts.** This is the most important difference.
`runcmd` runs late, and it races the kubelet. If `runcmd` loses that race,
containerd writes its state into the directory on the *root* disk. The array
mounts over that directory later, and the mount hides the data. The data still
uses space on the root disk, but no tool will ever find it. The node then
reports a full disk with no clear cause.

Corium builds arrays before it installs k0s. It also writes a drop-in so that
the k0s unit waits for the mount:

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/k0scontroller.service.d/10-corium-raid.conf
[Unit]
RequiresMountsFor=/var/lib/corium/data
```

The fstab entry has `nofail`. So if the array does not come back, the node still
boots and you can log in. Kubernetes refuses to start, with a clear error. It
does not run without its storage.

**It refuses to destroy data**, as described above. A `mdadm --create` command
that you write by hand does not ask.

**It is idempotent.** If you run the bootstrap twice, it adopts the array and
does not rebuild it. It rewrites its own fstab line and does not add a second
one.

### Checking an array

```bash
cat /proc/mdstat
sudo mdadm --detail /dev/md/data
findmnt /var/lib/corium/data
```

A healthy mirror shows `[UU]`. A degraded mirror shows `[U_]`. While degraded,
it continues to serve reads and writes.

### Replacing a failed disk

```bash
# 1. Remove the failed member.
sudo mdadm --manage /dev/md/data --remove /dev/disk/by-id/<failed>

# 2. Physically replace it, then add the new one.
sudo mdadm --manage /dev/md/data --add /dev/disk/by-id/<new>

# 3. Watch it rebuild.
cat /proc/mdstat
```

If you declare a `spares:` list, steps 1 and 2 happen automatically when a
member fails.

The node does not read the `corium:` block again after the first boot. So this
repair needs no configuration change. Also, a later change to the configuration
does not undo a manual repair.

## Root filesystem on RAID

> **Root-on-RAID needs three manual steps that Anaconda does not do for you. If
> you skip one, the machine does not survive the loss of its first disk.**
> Anaconda alone gives you a mirrored filesystem, not a redundant boot. We
> tested the procedure below from end to end on a two-disk machine. The test
> included removing the first disk and booting from the second. Corium does not
> model this in the `corium:` block, because the root filesystem is already
> mounted when the node reads that block.

You make this decision at install time, from the ISO. It is not available on
the qcow2 or cloud-image paths, because those ship a fixed disk layout.

### Worth weighing first

A cluster that can lose a node does not need nodes that can lose a disk. When a
disk fails, it is usually cheaper to provision the node again. The rest of
Corium uses that model, and the image-based upgrade path makes it fast.

Root-on-RAID gives you a root filesystem that survives. At present, it does not
reliably give you a boot without interruption.

### What is already in place

The image needs nothing added:

- `mdadm` ships in `fedora-bootc`.
- `mdadm` and its systemd units are in the initramfs. This lets the system
  assemble an array early enough to mount root from it.
- The Anaconda installer runtime includes `mdadm`. Its storage module processes
  `part` and `raid` for all payloads that install the OS.

### `/boot` on RAID1 is fine

The Anaconda GRUB2 backend accepts `mdarray` for `/boot`, only at RAID1, with
metadata `0.90`, `1.0` or `1.2`. Members must be partitions, not whole disks.
`GRUB2.install()` then installs to each disk under the array. So you can boot a
mirrored `/boot` from either disk.

### Do not put `/boot/efi` on RAID

**Use one independent, non-RAID ESP per disk.** `bootupd` expects this model.
It goes from `/boot` to the physical disks, and it finds the ESP on each disk. A
RAID1 `/boot` gives it both disks automatically.

<details>
<summary>Why, given that Anaconda accepts an ESP on RAID1</summary>

Anaconda allows it. `platform.py` lists `mdarray` with
`PLATFORM_RAID_LEVELS: [RAID1]` and `PLATFORM_RAID_METADATA: ["1.0"]`. blivet
forces metadata 1.0 for that mount point, because firmware cannot read 1.1 or
1.2. So the install does not reject the layout.

The failure comes later, and only on bootc. `bootupd` finds the ESP partition
from `/sys/class/block/<name>/partition`. An md device does not have this
attribute, so the installation stops:

```
error: boot data installation failed: installing component EFI:
Updating EFI firmware variables: Adding new EFI boot entry:
Failed to read /sys/class/block/md125/partition: No such file or directory
```

</details>

### Kickstart

`bootc-image-builder` embeds a kickstart into an `anaconda-iso` build. It adds
only the `ostreecontainer` line. You must supply the partitioning, network,
locale, and users. You cannot combine a `[customizations.installer.kickstart]`
block with other installer customizations.

> **Note.** This procedure uses the `anaconda-iso` type. Upstream deprecated
> that type, and also `bootc-image-builder`. The kickstart below stays when the
> ISO moves to its successor. It becomes a file in an installer container, not
> a build configuration. At that time, we will test it again and rewrite this
> section. Until then, this is the tested procedure. See
> [ADR 9](/docs/decisions/adr-0009-image-builder/).

> **Warning.** This kickstart alone is not sufficient. An install from it boots,
> but it does not survive the loss of its first disk. You must also do three
> manual steps, which are below. Build a second ESP in `%post`. Keep all work
> that is not disk-level out of `%post`. Add `nofail` to `/boot/efi` in
> `/etc/fstab`.

```toml
# config.toml
[customizations.installer.kickstart]
contents = """
text --non-interactive
zerombr
clearpart --all --initlabel --disklabel=gpt
ignoredisk --only-use=sda,sdb

# One ESP, on the first disk. The second one is built in %post, because
# Anaconda has no kickstart idiom for an unmounted ESP.
part /boot/efi --fstype=efi --size=600 --ondisk=sda

# /boot mirrored, metadata 1.2, members are partitions.
part raid.11 --size=2048 --ondisk=sda --fstype=mdmember
part raid.12 --size=2048 --ondisk=sdb --fstype=mdmember
raid /boot --level=RAID1 --device=boot --fstype=ext4 raid.11 raid.12

# Root mirrored. Sized rather than grown, so space is left at the end of the
# second disk for the ESP that %post creates there.
part raid.21 --size=16384 --ondisk=sda --fstype=mdmember
part raid.22 --size=16384 --ondisk=sdb --fstype=mdmember
raid / --level=RAID1 --device=root --fstype=ext4 raid.21 raid.22

lang en_US.UTF-8
keyboard us
timezone UTC --utc
network --bootproto=dhcp --device=link --activate --onboot=on
reboot
"""
```

Anaconda requires `--fstype=mdmember` on the members. Use `--device=<name>`, not
`--device=md0`, because the value is a name, not a device node. There is no
`--metadata` option. blivet selects the metadata.

### The three steps Anaconda leaves to you

An install with the kickstart above boots correctly. But it does not survive the
loss of the first disk. We found each step below when we removed the disk and
watched the result.

**1. Build a second ESP and register it.** Anaconda creates one ESP, on the
first disk. It gives this warning during the install:

```
boot loader stage2 device boot is on a multi-disk array, but boot loader
stage1 device sda1 is not. A drive failure in boot could render the system
unbootable.
```

The warning is correct. Without a second ESP, the firmware reports
`No bootable option or device was found` and stops.

Kickstart has no idiom for a second, unmounted ESP. Anaconda reads `part none
--fstype=efi` as a mount point with the name `none`, and the install fails when
it binds `/mnt/sysimagenone`. So size the last RAID member, and do not grow it.
This leaves space on the second disk. Then build the ESP in `%post`:

```bash
%post --nochroot
sgdisk --new=3:0:+600M --typecode=3:EF00 /dev/sdb
partprobe /dev/sdb; sleep 2
mkfs.vfat -F32 /dev/sdb3
mkdir -p /tmp/esp2 && mount /dev/sdb3 /tmp/esp2
cp -a /mnt/sysimage/boot/efi/. /tmp/esp2/
sync; umount /tmp/esp2
efibootmgr --create --disk /dev/sdb --part 3 \
  --label "Fedora (mirror)" --loader '\EFI\fedora\shimx64.efi'
%end
```

**2. Do the rest outside `%post`.** On a bootc install, files that `%post`
writes into `/mnt/sysimage/etc` and `/mnt/sysimage/var` do not survive.
Disk-level work survives. This is why the block above contains only `sgdisk`,
`mkfs` and `efibootmgr`. In our test, a `sudoers` drop-in and a log file written
the same way both disappeared without an error.

**3. Add `nofail` to `/boot/efi` in `/etc/fstab`.** It is easy to miss this
step. The machine boots correctly until the first disk fails. Then it goes into
emergency mode, although its mirrored filesystems are healthy and mounted. This
is the cause:

```
$ systemctl show boot-efi.mount -p RequiredBy -p WantedBy
RequiredBy=local-fs.target
WantedBy=
```

fstab mounts `/boot/efi` by the UUID of the ESP on the *first* disk. If that
disk fails, the mount fails. The mount is `RequiredBy` and not `WantedBy`. So
`local-fs.target` also fails, and systemd goes into emergency mode. When you add
`nofail`, the relation changes:

```
RequiredBy=
WantedBy=local-fs.target
```

On bootc, `/etc` is persistent and gets a three-way merge. So this change
survives image upgrades.

### Verified

With all three steps in place, we detached the first disk. The machine booted
from the second disk alone:

```
md126 : active raid1 sda2[1]
      2094080 blocks super 1.2 [2/1] [_U]     → /boot
md127 : active raid1 sda1[1]
      16759808 blocks super 1.2 [2/1] [_U]    → /sysroot

$ systemctl is-system-running
degraded
$ findmnt /boot/efi
(not mounted — its disk is gone)
```

The node started, accepted SSH, and `bootc status` still answered. The arrays
were degraded and continued to serve data. That is the purpose of a mirror.

### Rough edges that remain

- **`bootc-generic-growpart.service` fails on every boot.** It finds the
  partition from `/sys/class/block/<name>/partition`, and an md device does not
  have this file: `cat: /sys/class/block/md126/partition: No such file or
  directory`. The failure is not fatal. The unit fails and the system reports
  `degraded`, but everything else works. The same assumption breaks `bootupd`
  when the ESP itself is on RAID
  ([bootc#947](https://github.com/bootc-dev/bootc/discussions/947)). Set the
  size of the root array explicitly. Do not expect the unit to grow it.
- **After a failure, `/boot/efi` is not mounted.** The surviving ESP is present
  and the machine boots from it, but fstab still names the failed one. Change
  fstab to the surviving ESP before the next `bootc upgrade`. If you do not,
  bootloader updates have no target.
- **We did not test ESP synchronization during an update.** `bootupd` v0.2.28+
  updates every ESP it finds
  ([bootupd#855](https://github.com/coreos/bootupd/pull/855)), and this image
  includes v0.2.35. But
  [bootupd#1076](https://github.com/coreos/bootupd/issues/1076) is still open.
  In that issue, secondary ESPs do not receive `grub.cfg`. After your first
  upgrade, remove a disk and test again. A test after the install alone is not
  sufficient.

### What does not apply

People often quote these problems together, as if root-on-RAID cannot work.
Read them one at a time:

| Problem | Where | Applies? |
|---|---|---|
| `bootupctl` fails on an mdraid ESP | [bootc#947](https://github.com/bootc-dev/bootc/discussions/947) | **No.** That report put `/boot/efi` on RAID. The layout on this page does not, on purpose |
| Installing across multiple parent devices | [bootc#1911](https://github.com/bootc-dev/bootc/pull/1911) | **No.** Shipped in bootc v1.15.1. This image includes v1.16.10 |
| Updating every ESP, not just the booted one | [bootupd#855](https://github.com/coreos/bootupd/pull/855) | **No.** Shipped in bootupd v0.2.28. This image includes v0.2.35 |
| A custom kickstart's partitioning silently ignored | [bib#695](https://github.com/osbuild/bootc-image-builder/issues/695) | We did not see it, but make sure that `lsblk` shows the layout you expect |

Fedora CoreOS solves this with a declaration: Ignition's `boot_device.mirror`.
It builds the array in the initramfs and copies `/boot` to each disk. bootc has
no equivalent. Because of that gap, and not because of this repository,
`raid[]` covers only spare disks.

---

## What RAID is not

**It is not a backup.** A mirror copies an `rm -rf` to both disks as fast as it
copies all other writes. It protects against a disk failure, and against
nothing else.

**It is not cluster redundancy.** If you lose a node, you lose its workloads,
whether its disks were mirrored or not. If the data is important, keep it in a
place that survives the node. For example, use object storage, a replicated
volume, or a backup that you restored at least once.

An array is useful for local state that is expensive to rebuild and cheap to
keep. Examples are a large image cache, a local persistent volume behind a
service that is already replicated, and scratch space that you do not want to
lose during a job.
